ai.definition: Launch vehicles are spacecraft designed and used for transporting payloads into space. They can be expendable or reusable depending on the technology employed.
ai.howItWorks: Reusable rocket technology involves designing rockets that can land safely after their initial launch, allowing them to be refueled and reused multiple times. This reduces overall costs associated with launching payloads into orbit by eliminating the need for building a new rocket for each mission.
ai.problemSolved: High costs of space launches due to the expendability of current rockets. Reusable rockets can significantly reduce these costs, making space exploration more accessible.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing reusable launch vehicles requires advanced materials and precise engineering. The process involves designing lightweight yet robust rocket components, integrating sophisticated propulsion systems, and developing automated landing technologies.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with detailed design phases followed by component manufacturing. Next, assembly of the rocket occurs in clean rooms to ensure no contamination. Finally, extensive testing is conducted before the vehicle undergoes its maiden flight.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include material costs for advanced alloys and composites, R&D expenses, and operational costs such as landing site maintenance and crew training. The cost of refurbishment between launches also plays a significant role in overall economics.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: As of now, reusable launch vehicles are being tested and refined by various private companies and government agencies. Commercial applications are expected to increase as the technology matures and becomes more cost-effective.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary widely across countries but generally involve safety standards, environmental impact assessments, and licensing requirements for launches. International agreements may also apply regarding space debris and orbital traffic management.
ai.risks: Risks include technical challenges in achieving reliable landings, potential damage to the rocket during reuse cycles, and operational risks such as launch failures or malfunctions during re-entry.
ai.profitability: Profitability is highly dependent on mission frequency and payload value. While initial investments are substantial, reusable rockets can reduce costs per flight significantly, making them potentially profitable over time with high demand for launches.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development focuses on further improving reliability, increasing payload capacity, and reducing turnaround times between flights. Advancements in AI and automation could also enhance the efficiency of launch preparation processes.

glossary.def: A spacecraft capable of returning to Earth after a mission and being prepared for another launch.
The engine or engines that provide thrust for the rocket, enabling it to reach space.
The maximum mass or volume that a spacecraft can carry into orbit or beyond.

subsystems.name: Propulsion
subsystems.role: generates thrust and steers the rocket by gimballing the engines.
parts: main engines (kerosene, methane or hydrogen with liquid oxygen)
regeneratively cooled combustion chamber and nozzle

subsystems.name: Structures and propellant tanks
subsystems.role: a lightweight shell strong enough to hold hundreds of tonnes of cryogenic propellant.

subsystems.name: Avionics and guidance
subsystems.role: flies the ascent trajectory and keeps the vehicle stable through Max-Q.

subsystems.name: Stage separation
subsystems.role: jettisons the spent lower stage cleanly at high speed.

subsystems.name: Payload accommodation
subsystems.role: protects the satellite and releases it in the right orbit.

subsystems.name: Recovery system (reusable vehicles)
subsystems.role: brings the first stage back for refurbishment and reuse.
parts: reserve propellant for a landing burn

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: everything needed before the countdown reaches zero.

buildSteps.title: Set the mission requirements
buildSteps.detail: Target orbit and payload mass dictate how many stages, which propellants and roughly how large the vehicle must be.

buildSteps.title: Design stage by stage
buildSteps.detail: Engineers trade propellant type, mass ratio and engine count; the rocket equation decides how much of the launch mass must be propellant.

buildSteps.title: Build the engines
buildSteps.detail: Turbopump impellers, injectors, chambers and nozzles are machined and welded, then each engine is fired on a test stand to measure thrust and specific impulse.

buildSteps.title: Make the tanks
buildSteps.detail: Thin-gauge metal panels are formed, friction-stir welded into barrels and domes, and pressure-tested. Methane-fuelled vehicles use stainless steel; others use aluminium–lithium or composites.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and test a stage
buildSteps.detail: Engines, tanks, plumbing, avionics and wiring are mated; the stage then undergoes cryogenic proof and static-fire testing.

buildSteps.title: Stack the vehicle
buildSteps.detail: Stages are stacked vertically in an assembly building or on the pad, and the encapsulated payload is added on top.

buildSteps.title: Rehearse the countdown
buildSteps.detail: Propellant loading, hold-down tests and software rehearsals exercise every system before launch day.

buildSteps.title: Launch and ascend
buildSteps.detail: The vehicle lifts off, performs a gravity turn, throttles through maximum aerodynamic pressure, then separates stages and coasts to orbit.

buildSteps.title: Recover or expend
buildSteps.detail: A reusable booster re-enters, steers with grid fins and lands under engine power; expendable stages burn up or are left in a graveyard orbit.

prerequisites.why: the only propulsion with enough thrust-to-weight and efficiency to reach orbit.
every kilogram of dry mass is a kilogram of payload lost.
the vehicle must fly a precise trajectory and stay stable in a constantly changing atmosphere.

prerequisites.tech: Reusable thermal protection and propulsive landing
prerequisites.why: booster reuse is routine for some medium-lift vehicles, but full-vehicle reuse is still in flight testing.
cryogenic propellants and range safety require purpose-built, remotely located sites.

pathway.milestone: routine first-stage propulsive landing and reflight
pathway.unlocks: lower cost per kilogram and much higher launch cadence.

pathway.milestone: fully reusable super-heavy vehicles reaching orbit and returning both stages
pathway.unlocks: aircraft-like turnaround and a further step-change in launch cost.

pathway.milestone: reliable high-cadence launch to low Earth orbit
pathway.unlocks: large satellite constellations and cheap science missions.
heavy payloads beyond low Earth orbit and crewed deep-space missions without expending whole vehicles.
